item.title: Tonga faces severe drought threat as El Niño brings very dry conditions nationwide

item.content:encoded:
Tonga is facing the prospect of a severe and prolonged drought, with the Tonga Meteorological Service warning that a strong to very strong El Niño could bring very dry conditions across the entire country and place growing pressure on water supplies, food production and public health.

The Meteorological Drought Outlook issued on 18 August 2026 says El Niño is already underway in Tonga and the tropical Pacific, with forecasts pointing to an event that could rank among the strongest observed since 1950. El Niño conditions typically bring below-average rainfall and the possibility of prolonged drought in Tonga.

The warning comes as Tonga is already experiencing widespread dryness. In July, dry conditions were observed across all of Tonga, with very dry conditions in Vava’u and seriously dry conditions in Tongatapu and ‘Eua. Over the three months from May to July, dry conditions were recorded across all island groups, with seriously dry conditions in Ha’apai, Tongatapu and ‘Eua.

The outlook for the coming months is even more concerning.

Very dry conditions are forecast across all of Tonga in August, with a 70 to 80 per cent chance in Niuafo’ou and Niuatoputapu, 50 to 70 per cent in Tongatapu and ‘Eua, and 40 to 50 per cent in Ha’apai and Vava’u.

For August to October, the chance of very dry conditions rises to between 80 and 100 per cent across all of Tonga.

The drought outlook shows the situation worsening in several island groups by the end of October. Niuafo’ou is forecast to move from Drought Alert to Drought Declaration, while Niuatoputapu is expected to remain under Drought Declaration after escalating from Drought Warning. Vava’u is forecast to progress from Drought Alert to Drought Declaration.

Ha’apai, Tongatapu and ‘Eua are already at Drought Declaration and are expected to remain there through October.

The outlook identifies reduced or empty water tanks within one month, followed by depleted groundwater, including on Tongatapu, and drying bore and well water. It also warns of increased costs for pumping and drinking water, as well as increased water salinity.

The impacts could become more severe if dry conditions persist, with competing demands for water from households, agriculture and livestock.

Agriculture is also expected to come under increasing pressure as soil moisture declines.

The Meteorological Service identifies impacts on yams, cassava and taro, along with reduced breadfruit and pineapple yields. Kava growth could be reduced, while cattle and pigs could also be affected by reduced pasture availability and increased demand for drinking water.

The outlook also warns of reduced crop production, higher crop prices, increased irrigation demand and impacts on livelihoods and food security.

The drought could also create serious health and hygiene problems.

The outlook identifies dehydration, skin disease, nose bleeding, fever, vomiting and breathing difficulties associated with prolonged drought. Reduced access to water for sanitation and hygiene could increase infectious diseases, including typhoid, diarrhoea and lung disease.

Vulnerable people, including people with disabilities in the outer islands, could face reduced access to water. The outlook also warns that hospitals and emergency centres could run out of water if the drought persists.

The effects could extend well beyond households and farms.

The Meteorological Service identifies potential disruption to household incomes and livelihoods, increased demands for drought relief, higher shipping costs and increased pressure on water facilities.

Schools could also be affected, particularly in the outer islands, with reduced water supplies potentially affecting students’ focus and performance. Prolonged drought could lead to lower attendance, dropouts and school closures.

The outlook also warns of an increased risk of wildfires, while power supplies could be disrupted by limited water available for cooling equipment. Fire Services may need to use seawater.

The Meteorological Service notes that the impacts are based on stakeholder consultation and are estimates of when impacts may become evident following below-average rainfall. The severity of impacts can vary according to island size, topography, geology and soil type.

With very dry conditions forecast across every island group and the drought outlook showing further escalation through October, the warning is that Tonga’s dry spell could become a much broader threat to water security, food production, health and livelihoods.

item.title: NZ fur seal stranded on remote Ha'apai island released at sea
item.description: A New Zealand fur seal that was stranded in a remote island in Ha'apai has been released at sea after spending four days in the care of a local fisherman. The rare visitor came ashore on Tokulu, a small limestone island located between the remote islands of Tungua and Nomuka.
item.content:encoded:
A New Zealand fur seal that was stranded in a remote island in Ha'apai has been released at sea after spending four days in the care of a local fisherman.

The rare visitor came ashore on Tokulu, a small limestone island located between the remote islands of Tungua and Nomuka.

Fisherman Sione Meiha’amoa (Toa) told Matangi Tonga that he discovered the juvenile seal stranded on Tokulu last Wednesday, 12 August, and brought it back to his home island of Tungua.

" I found it stranded ashore on Tokulu," Toa said.

The seal remained inland for four days while Toa cared for it before it was released at sea on Sunday, 16 August, to continue its journey.

Toa said a group from New Zealand was contacted through the Prime Minister’s Office to assess the seal. He understood from the group that the animal was about one year old and still a juvenille. He was also told that it had come from New Zealand.

" They were concerned for the animal and wanted me to release it."

Toa said he was told he could face a fine of $10,000 pa'anga if he did not release the seal.

The young fur seal has now been returned to the sea, with hopes that it will make its way back towards its natural habitat.

New Zealand fur seals are not naturally found in Tonga, where tropical waters are far outside the species' usual cold and temperate habitat.

Sightings of seals in Tonga are rare, although similar unusual appearances have been recorded in Tonga, Fiji, Cook Islands, and Tahiti over the years.

The unusual arrival comes as Tonga has experienced periods of colder-than-usual weather in recent months.

The New Zealand Department of Conservation ( DOC ) website states that Kekeno are the most common seals in New Zealand and their population is growing. They are usually found on rocky shores throughout mainland New Zealand, the Chatham Islands, and the subantarctic islands, as well as parts of Australia .

Seals are very good swimmers and weaned pups will sometimes travel great distances. On land seals have been found in unusual places such as backyards, drains and streets.

“Despite these odd appearances, seals are best left alone with no human intervention.”

Fur seals and sea lions are distinguished from other seals by their external ear flaps and hind flippers which rotate forward, allowing them to move quickly on land.

New Zealand fur seals can be distinguished from sea lions by their pointy nose and smaller size.

This pointy-nosed seal has long pale whiskers and a body covered with two layers of fur. Their coat is dark grey-brown on the back, and lighter below.

Adult females grow to a maximum length 1.5 m, weight 30-50 kg, while adult males grow to amaximum length 2.5 m, weight 90-150 kg.

From birth to weaning Pups are suckled for about 300 days, though some will continue to suckle into their second year. During spring most pups are weaned and disperse. Juvenile fur seals have been found over 1000 km away from their place of birth.

item.title: Pacific Brewing Tonga relaunches
item.description: Pacific Brewing Tonga officially reopened at the Small Industries Centre in Nuku'alofa on Saturday, beginning a new chapter for the local brewery after almost a year of closure and restructuring. The brewery closed in October 2025 after the brewer Alo Fe’iloakitau became ill. He passed away in February this year.
item.content:encoded:
Pacific Brewing Tonga officially reopened at the Small Industries Centre in Nuku'alofa on Saturday, beginning a new chapter for the local brewery after almost a year of closure and restructuring.

The brewery closed in October 2025 after the brewer Alo Fe’iloakitau became ill. He passed away in February this year.

CEO Tricia Emberson said Fe’iloakitau had been the “heart” of the business, helping run the brewery and dedicating much of his life to its development.

The business had survived the challenges of the COVID -19 pandemic before his illness forced its closure.

Emberson said she initially considered selling the brewery or walking away after his death.

“I walked in here one day and I stood and I looked at these tanks and I thought, I can’t do this,” she said.

However, encouragement from supporters and members of the community prompted a decision to rebuild the brewery and continue its operations.

The relaunch includes fresh investment, new products and additional brewing expertise, with the business now employing an all-Tongan female workforce and a predominantly female management team.

Australian brewers Richard Addison, from Young Henrys, and Sean Listed, from Playwood Brewing and Gilmore, have joined the project, working alongside Pacific Brewing's local team and helping train staff.

The reopening faced several technical setbacks, including a boiler failure during the rebuilding process and a subsequent leak in the glycol chiller used to maintain beer at the required temperature.

The local team worked with Australian and regional brewing technicians through video calls and received technical assistance from Fiji Breweries.

Emberson said the collaboration helped prevent the first batches of beer from being lost.

“It’s been a really collaborative effort to get us all here,” she said.

The first products released following the reopening include Maui Naga and Tiki Pacific Ale, while the company is developing ready-to-drink beverages under the 676 brand, including vodka spritzers.

Pacific Brewing is currently bottling its products locally and is exploring local canning options.

An initial batch of cans will be produced in Australia before the company aims to move can manufacturing to Tonga.

The brewery also plans to expand exports across the Pacific and into international markets.

Emberson said the long-term goal was for Pacific Brewing products to carry the Tongan flag and be proudly marketed as “Made in Tonga”.

She said that continued government support, investment and training would be needed to ensure local workers could maintain production standards.

“Maybe in the process it means jobs, it means training, it means investment, and it means opportunities staying here in the Kingdom,” she said.

The company is also planning a bottle and can recycling programme and has introduced staff training initiatives.

Emberson said the reopening was personally significant and represented a way of continuing Fe’iloakitau's work and legacy.

“For me personally, seeing beer coming out of these tanks again is emotional,” she said.

“I believe the best way of moving on from everything he put into this brewery is not simply to let it end when he passed, but to ensure this brewery has a future.”

The relaunch concluded with the first beers poured from the brewery's tanks for guests to taste.

The event brought together local business owners, Australian co-investors and brewing specialists, government representatives and invited guests.

Pacific Brewing is supporting a programme assisting individuals and families affected by addiction in Tonga, Fiji and Australia.

Prop idol has his 'mojo' back - and Wallabies want more
item.description: Wallabies coach Les Kiss will stay in regular touch with Taniela Tupou's French club to ensure the in-form prop remains a regular fixture. Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled how the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.
item.content:encoded:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss will stay in regular touch with Taniela Tupou's French club to ensure the in-form prop remains a regular fixture.

Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled how the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.

Tupou scored two first-half tries for Australia, who trailed before scoring 42 consecutive points in a 56-17 defeat of Japan in Townsville on Saturday.

All three starting front-rowers, as well as replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa and back-rowers Harry Wilson and Charlie Cale, were Australia's try-scorers in Townsville.

Tupou scored the match-winner in Osaka against Eddie Jones' men a week earlier after coming off the bench and has shown power and skill to indicate he's back near his best approaching next year's home Rugby World Cup.

" He's found a little bit of himself again, and he's been more of himself," Wallabies coach Kiss said, while also noting his combination with good mate and returning lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto.

" I'm very, very big on making sure the players be themselves as much as possible."

Former Queensland Reds star Tupou agonised over his move from Australian rugby to France, with Racing 92 last season but it's helped him turn back the clock after several underwhelming seasons at the Melbourne Rebels and NSW Waratahs.

" Moving to France, he's found out who he is a little bit more and he's come back and he's really connected with the group here and found that bit of mojo that he likes to thrive on," Kiss said.

With English-based Tom Hooper yet to return to the side, Tupou is the only overseas-based Wallaby currently in the Test rotation.

The coach has remained in touch with Racing 92's staff to ensure they have his services for the two-Test tour of Argentina that begins later this month and hopefully beyond.

" All good, as I believe, at this stage.

" I'll be talking to the coach and the team manager of Racing, this week, again, to make sure they understand how we're looking after Nella and making sure we're doing the right thing with him and working him hard.

" So they can trust the process as well. But, yeah, he'll be with us."

Jones joked post-game that Tupou played as if there was a pizza on offer for every try and reckoned he would even deliver one to the change-rooms himself.

" No pizza, I'll have to hit him up about that one," Tupou grinned.

" I've got a lot of love and respect for Eddie, actually. Nothing against that, he loves me, I know that."

Tupou said he wanted to "take it to the next level" after finding his feet in France.

And he said Kiss's tweaks were helping him get there.

" To get the ball in my hands as a forward, less running without the ball, more running with it," Tupou said.

" We're still working on it, but it's good to see forwards scoring tries."

item.title: China pushes back on US-led call for advance notice of future missile tests
item.description: Chinese diplomats have pushed back on a joint statement signed by 40 countries, following a Chinese SLBM missile test in the Pacific Islands, with Australia, New Zealand, the Marshall Islands and Palau joining a US -led call for advance notice for future launches. The Chinese say there is a double standard in the demands.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese diplomats have pushed back on a joint statement signed by 40 countries, following a Chinese SLBM missile test in the Pacific Islands, with Australia, New Zealand, the Marshall Islands and Palau joining a US -led call for advance notice for future launches.

The Chinese say there is a double standard in the demands.

China tested a submarine-launched ballistic missile ( SLBM ) into the Pacific Ocean on July 6, 2026. The missile carried a dummy warhead and landed in international open waters in the South Pacific.

The US -led statement of 11 August called for "all relevant countries" to commit to providing no less than 24 hours' notice of launches of intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles to affected nations.

Ambassador Li Chijiang, China’s Ambassador for Disarmament Affairs at a Conference on Disarmament last week said the US demand had no legal basis, because t he Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (“ HCOC ”) is not a universally joined mechanism. “China, as a non-member of the HCOC , is not bound by it.”

However, he said that 24 hours prior to China’s test launch in July this year, China had provided pre-launch notifications to other nuclear-weapon states, including the U.S., Russia, the U.K., and France, as well as Japan, the Republic of Korea, Australia, New Zealand and other Pacific island countries around the missile impact area.

To date, China has conducted only three ICBM launch tests.

He alleged that “The U.S. has conducted over 300 ICBM test launches and about 200 SLBM test launches, and most of its ICBM test launches have taken place in the Pacific Ocean.

“But the U.S. has not provided China with advance notifications in recent years, except on only one occasion.”

The only regional signatories to the US -led statement were Palau, which is hosting the Pacific Islands Forum in September, the Marshall Islands, Australia and New Zealand.

Tonga did not sign the US -led statement and, like other Pacific Islands states, has not overtly criticised the Chinese missile test, while making carefully crafted diplomatic statements..

On 23 July Tonga's Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua highlighted China's duty in Pacific countries to ensure our shared regional environment is one that is “safe and secure”.

He was speaking at a reception in Nuku'alofa to celebrate the 99 th anniversary of Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

Lord Fakafanua said Tonga and the People's Republic of China had enduring diplomatic relations and long standing partnership.

“These ever-shifting ties embody the partnership, its resilience, and transformation while also highlighting China's growing duty in Pacific countries, like Tonga, to ensure our shared regional environment is one that is safe and secure, especially where international peacekeeping and humanitarian support prevails.”

He said Tonga was committed to peaceful dialogue and principled multilateralism, whether through the Pacific Islands Forum, or the United Nations.

“Such multilateral and regional institutions are needed now more than ever. The global uncertainties of today demand that these are the cornerstones of our foreign engagement,” Lord Fakafanua said.

At the function hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Tonga, Ambassador H.E. Liu Weimin, said that China respected the aspirations of regional countries to maintain the South Pacific as a nuclear free zone.

item.title: Blue Transformation, the Pacific Way: Communities, Ocean and the Future of Aquatic Food Systems
item.description: For Pacific Island peoples, the ocean was never simply a resource to be managed — it is vanua, fonua, aiga, whenua moana: ancestor, provider, pathway and identity, bound together in systems of reciprocity that long predate the language of “blue economy” or “aquatic food systems.” Long before global institutions spoke of sustainable ocean governance, Pacific communities were already practising it —
item.content:encoded:
For Pacific Island peoples, the ocean was never simply a resource to be managed — it is vanua, fonua, aiga, whenua moana: ancestor, provider, pathway and identity, bound together in systems of reciprocity that long predate the language of “blue economy” or “aquatic food systems.” Long before global institutions spoke of sustainable ocean governance, Pacific communities were already practising it — through tabu areas and rahui, customary marine tenure, seasonal fishing calendars and knowledge passed down through generations of navigators, fisherfolk and reef custodians.

Today, as the world grapples with climate change, population growth and food insecurity, global attention has turned to what the Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO ) calls “Blue Transformation” the idea that aquatic food systems must grow sustainably, nourish people, generate livelihoods and protect ocean ecosystems. The Pacific region, framed by our leaders not as a scatter of “small island states” but as the Blue Pacific Continent, is central to this conversation. It is global framework which is finally catching up to what Pacific communities have long known, and whether they can be reshaped to serve Pacific priorities, in Pacific way.

An ocean of identity, not just an asset class

The Pacific covers roughly a third of the Earth’s surface, and stewards some of the richest tuna resources, most diverse reef systems and most extensive exclusive economic zones on the planet. Home to some of the world’s richest tuna resources and vast ocean territories, Pacific countries have long demonstrated that economic development and ocean stewardship can go hand in hand. Yet the challenges remain significant. Small island developing states face increasing climate risks, fragile supply chains, high dependence on food imports and growing pressure on marine ecosystems.

The 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, endorsed by Pacific Islands Forum Leaders, is explicit that ocean health, food security and cultural identity are inseparable — this is not simply an environmental or economic policy question, but one of survival, sovereignty and wellbeing for atoll nations, high islands and everything in between.

FAO ’s latest State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture ( SOFIA ) report confirms that global fish production has reached record levels and that aquaculture is now among the fastest-growing food sectors worldwide — but it also warns that many marine resources remain under strain and sustainability remains a major concern and that improved management is essential to secure future benefits. For Pacific nations already living with coral bleaching, ocean acidification, sea-level rise and more intense cyclones, this warning is not abstract. It shapes what ends up on the table in a household in communities or lands in local markets, or a canoe returning to shore in the outer islands.

Community-led and technically supported – a win-win pathway

Where Blue Transformation succeeds in the Pacific, it tends to succeed because it starts with communities, not around them. Small-scale and subsistence fishers, often women, who dominate near-shore gleaning and post- harvest processing across much of Melanesia, Polynesia and Micronesia, remain the backbone of food security and coastal livelihoods, even though their labour is frequently undercounted in national statistics. Any strategy for resilient aquatic food systems has to be built around their knowledge, their access to markets and infrastructure, and their authority over adjacent waters, not treat them as beneficiaries of a plan designed without listening to them.

This is where locally led initiatives are already showing the way. For Pacific nations, this message is particularly relevant. Sustainable ocean management is not simply an environmental issue; it is a matter of food security, economic sovereignty and resilience. Healthy fish stocks support coastal communities, generate public revenues and provide one of the most nutritious sources of protein available. This is where FAO ’s Blue Transformation agenda becomes especially important.

Through its global roadmap, FAO promotes three mutually reinforcing objectives: sustainable aquaculture growth, effective fisheries management and more efficient aquatic food value chains. These priorities are highly aligned with the needs and aspirations of Pacific Island countries.

Across the Pacific, FAO is already supporting innovation and transformation. Countries including Kiribati, Palau, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Solomon Islands and Nauru are advancing digital agriculture and fisheries strategies designed to strengthen productivity, improve market access and increase resilience against climate shocks. In Fiji, initiatives connecting farmers, fishers, tourism operators and local markets help create stronger local food systems while reducing dependence on imports.

SOFIA also highlights the critical role these fishers play in nutrition, employment and local development. Ensuring that they have access to markets, infrastructure, technology and social protection is essential for building inclusive and resilient aquatic food systems.

Climate change adds urgency to this agenda. Rising sea levels, coral bleaching, ocean warming and increasingly extreme weather events threaten both food production and livelihoods throughout the Pacific. Yet aquatic food systems can also become part of the solution. Sustainable fisheries, responsible aquaculture and healthy marine ecosystems contribute to climate adaptation, biodiversity conservation and more resilient local economies. SOFIA emphasizes that aquatic food systems can provide important environmental and climate solutions when managed effectively.

The Pacific has often been described as “large ocean states” rather than “small island states.” This perspective captures an important truth: the region possesses enormous ocean assets and extraordinary expertise in managing them. The future of Blue Transformation will depend not only on global commitments but also on local leadership, indigenous knowledge and regional cooperation.

FAO ’s role is to support this journey by providing data, scientific evidence, technical assistance and policy guidance. Through SOFIA and other initiatives, the Organization continues to help countries understand emerging trends, identify opportunities and make informed decisions that balance economic growth with sustainability.

The message emerging from the latest SOFIA report is clear. The world needs more nutritious food, healthier oceans and stronger coastal economies. The Pacific Islands already possess many of the ingredients necessary to achieve these goals. By embracing Blue Transformation, the region can continue to lead globally in demonstrating that ocean prosperity and ocean stewardship are not competing objectives, but two sides of the same sustainable future.

In the decades ahead, the Pacific may not simply participate in Blue Transformation, it may well define what successful Blue Transformation looks like for the world.

Maurizio Martina is the Deputy Director General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations ( FAO ) responsible for overseeing strategic partnership, global cooperation, and corporate management. He is also a former Minister of Agriculture of Italy.
